heroIntro: A perennial source of bitter family conflict across Bangladesh occurs when joint ancestral property (Paitrik Sompotti) is left undivided following the demise of parents. Suddenly, one aggressive brother, uncle, or co-heir secretly negotiates with an outside developer or stranger, executes a registered sale deed for a specific prime portion of the family land or homestead, and pockets the cash without obtaining the consent of other siblings. The unsuspecting sisters, living elsewhere or abroad, return to find strangers erecting boundary walls across their childhood homestead. In Bangladesh, joint property rights are governed by clear statutory checks under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, the Partition Act 1893, and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. Understanding how to block unauthorized sales, enforce pre-emption rights, and institute Partition Suits is vital to protecting your rightful inheritance.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: Can a Co-Heir Legally Sell Ancestral Land Without Other Heirs' Consent in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: A co-heir (Warish) has the legal right to sell only their undivided, proportionate statutory share (Saham) of ancestral property, but they CANNOT sell any specific demarcated portion, nor can they sell another co-heir's share without written power of attorney. Crucially, under the second paragraph of Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, if an undivided share of an ancestral family dwelling house is sold to a stranger, the buyer does NOT acquire the right to joint possession or common enjoyment of the house. Other co-heirs can immediately file a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Civil Court under the Partition Act 1893, secure a Temporary Injunction (Order 39 CPC) halting all construction, and exercise statutory Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 to forcibly buy back the sold share.
highlights: A co-heir can only sell their undivided mathematical share, never a specific demarcated plot before formal partition.
Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 strictly prohibits outside buyers from taking joint possession of an ancestral dwelling house.
Co-sharers possess statutory Pre-emption rights under Section 96 of the SAT Act 1950 to repurchase the land from the stranger.
An immediate Partition Suit and Order 39 CPC injunction blocks the outside purchaser from altering or building on the land.
points: Step 1: Conduct a Sub-Registry Office search (Balam inspection) to obtain a certified copy of the unauthorized sale deed.
Step 2: File an urgent Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) before the Senior Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court.
Step 3: Move an emergency application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39 Rules 1-2 CPC to halt construction and possession.
Step 4: Exercise statutory Pre-emption under Section 96 SAT Act or Section 4 Partition Act 1893 to buy back the transferred share.

sections.title: The Ancestral Property Conflict in Bangladesh
sections.content:
In Bangladesh, land succession is governed by religious personal laws (Muslim Faraiz or Hindu Succession). Upon the demise of a parent, all surviving legal heirs automatically become joint tenants-in-common, owning undivided shares in every square inch of the estate. While this communal ownership reflects family solidarity, it frequently degenerates into predatory land grabs.

A pervasive problem occurs when one brother or male heir, residing on the physical property while sisters or other siblings live in different cities or abroad, treats the entire ancestral estate as his personal fiefdom. Needing money, he enters into private negotiations with aggressive developers or local influential buyers. Without consulting other co-sharers or initiating a formal partition, he executes a registered deed purporting to sell a specific prime roadside corner or residential portion of the homestead. The co-sharers are suddenly confronted with armed laborers fencing off their land. Understanding the legal limitations of joint ownership and the precise statutory remedies available is essential to halting this expropriation.

sections.title: Undivided Share vs. Specific Demarcation: The Legal Rule
sections.content:
The core legal principle governing joint property in Bangladesh is that prior to a formal, registered Deed of Partition (Aposh Batwara) or a civil court partition decree, no co-sharer owns any specific physical spot or boundary. Every co-heir holds an undivided fractional interest across the entire undivided parcel.

Consequently, under the Transfer of Property Act 1882, while a co-heir is legally entitled to alienate their undivided fractional share (e.g., their 4-anna or 25% mathematical entitlement), they have zero legal authority to sell a specific demarcated plot (such as 'the front 2 decimals facing the main road'). If an aggressive co-heir executes a deed specifically defining and transferring a particular physical parcel without the concurrence of other co-sharers, that specific demarcation is legally void against the non-consenting heirs. The purchaser merely steps into the shoes of the seller as an undivided co-sharer and cannot claim exclusive possession of any specific corner.

sections.title: Section 44 Transfer of Property Act: Dwelling House Shield
sections.content:
The legislature recognized that allowing third-party strangers into an undivided family homestead destroys family privacy and social peace. To prevent this, the second paragraph of Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 provides an extraordinary statutory shield:

'Where the transferee of a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family is not a member of the family, nothing in this section shall be deemed to entitle him to joint possession or other common or part enjoyment of the house.'

This statutory provision is of monumental importance. It establishes that even if a stranger holds a valid registered deed purchased from an unscrupulous co-heir, that stranger has absolutely no legal right to enter the family homestead, break locks, construct rooms, or reside on the premises. If the stranger attempts to force entry, they commit criminal trespass under Section 441 of the Penal Code 1860, and the civil court will grant an immediate injunction restraining them from entering the dwelling house.

sections.title: Statutory Pre-emption Rights Under SAT Act Section 96
sections.content:
When an ancestral co-heir sells their share to an outside stranger without offering it first to family members, the remaining co-heirs possess an aggressive statutory weapon: the right of Pre-emption (Ogrokroy). In Bangladesh, pre-emption is governed by Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (SAT Act) and Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893.

Under Section 96 SAT Act, if a portion or share of a holding of land is transferred to any person who is not a co-sharer in the holding, any co-sharer tenant has the legal right to apply to the civil court within two (2) months of the service of notice of transfer, or within two months of learning of the transfer, to have the transferred property forcibly re-transferred to themselves upon depositing the consideration money plus statutory compensation into court. Furthermore, under Section 4 of the Partition Act 1893, if the buyer of a dwelling house share sues for partition, the family members have the absolute statutory right to compel the court to value the share and allow the family to buy out the stranger, expelling them permanently from the ancestral home.

sections.title: Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) and Advocate Commissioners
sections.content:
The definitive, permanent legal remedy to resolve undivided ancestral land disputes is instituting a formal Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Civil Court having territorial jurisdiction. The suit proceeds in two distinct judicial phases:

  1. Preliminary Decree: The civil court examines the genealogy (Warishan tree), examines CS, SA, RS, and City/BS Khatians, and delivers a preliminary decree declaring the precise fractional share (Saham) belonging to each co-heir and setting aside any unauthorized demarcation.
  2. Appointment of Advocate Commissioner: Following the preliminary decree, the court appoints a neutral Advocate Commissioner accompanied by a government surveyor (Amin) to visit the physical land. The commissioner surveys the entire plot, evaluates road frontage, valuation, and existing possession, and drafts a scientific field demarcation (Batwara map) allocating separate physical plots to each co-heir.
  3. Final Decree: The court hears objections, approves the commissioner's report, and passes a Final Decree, permanently carving out separate, independent titles and boundaries for each heir, ending joint friction forever.

sections.title: Securing Emergency Injunctions Under Order 39 CPC
sections.content:
Because a Partition Suit takes time to conclude through trial and commission, the urgent battle is preserving the property in status quo. If the rogue buyer or aggressive co-heir rapidly cuts down ancestral fruit orchards, demolishes family structures, or erects commercial buildings, the character of the land is permanently altered.

Upon filing the Partition Suit, your advocate immediately submits an interlocutory petition for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The court evaluates whether the petitioner is an undisputed co-sharer and whether construction without formal partition causes irreparable harm. Upon satisfaction, the civil court grants an ad-interim injunction restraining all parties, including the outside buyer, from altering the physical character of the land, cutting trees, raising any construction, or executing further sale deeds until the disposal of the partition suit.

sections.title: Special Protection for Sisters and Overseas NRB Heirs
sections.content:
A notorious social injustice in Bangladesh involves male siblings disenfranchising their married sisters or overseas expatriate (NRB) brothers. Brothers frequently tell their sisters, 'Our father gave you gold at your wedding, so you have no claim on the land,' or they forge heirship certificates excluding sisters' names entirely to obtain fraudulent mutations (E-Namjari).

Under Islamic law and the statutory laws of Bangladesh, a daughter's right to inherit ancestral land from her parents is absolute, divine, and unalienable. Dowry or marriage gifts do not extinguish a daughter's statutory inheritance. If brothers forge a Warishan certificate or execute sale deeds concealing sisters, the sisters can institute criminal prosecution for forgery under Sections 467 and 468 of the Penal Code, cancel the fraudulent mutation via an E-Namjari Miss Case before the AC Land, and file a Partition Suit claiming their full Faraiz shares. For overseas Bangladeshis residing in the UK, USA, or Canada, these proceedings can be fully executed through a registered Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy.

sections.title: Comparison Table: Lawful Co-Heir Rights vs. Third-Party Buyer
sections.content:
The table below summarizes the legal rights of existing co-heirs versus an outside buyer who purchased an undivided share without unanimous consent:

The law firmly shields ancestral families against outside intrusion, subordinating the third-party buyer's interests to the comprehensive partition decree of the civil court.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Blocking an Illegal Ancestral Sale in Sylhet
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how joint heirs protected their ancestral homestead in Sylhet:

A deceased expatriate businessman left behind an undivided 24-decimal homestead in Beanibazar, Sylhet, inherited by three sons and two daughters. Two sons and both daughters lived abroad in London, while the eldest son remained in Sylhet managing the family home. In mid-2024, the eldest son incurred massive personal debts. Without informing his four expatriate siblings, he negotiated with a local commercial developer, executed a registered Saf Kabala deed purporting to sell the entire front 10 decimals facing the highway, and received BDT 60,00,000.

Two months later, the London-based siblings were alerted by relatives that the developer had brought bulldozers to level the front garden and construct a commercial shopping complex. Acting swiftly through a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh High Commission in London, the siblings engaged a Supreme Court advocate. The legal team immediately obtained certified copies of the sale deed, which revealed that the brother had purported to sell a demarcated roadside parcel exceeding his mathematical Faraiz share.

The advocate filed an urgent Partition Suit in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Sylhet, coupled with an interlocutory petition under Order 39 Rules 1-2 CPC and Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act. The judge issued an immediate status quo injunction restraining all construction and prohibiting the developer from entering the homestead. Concurrently, the advocate filed a Pre-emption case under Section 96 SAT Act depositing the statutory funds into the treasury. Faced with an unyielding judicial injunction and the certainty of pre-emption buyout, the developer terminated the transaction, the brother was compelled to refund the funds, and the court proceeded with a formal preliminary partition decree securing all five siblings' equal rights.

faqs.question: Can a brother sell ancestral property without his sisters' permission in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: A brother can sell only his own undivided share (Saham) calculated under Islamic Faraiz rules. He cannot sell his sisters' shares, nor can he sell any specific demarcated portion of the property without their formal written consent or a registered partition deed.

faqs.question: What is Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882?
faqs.answer: Section 44 protects undivided family dwelling houses. It explicitly dictates that if an outsider buys an undivided share of an ancestral family home, the buyer does NOT acquire the right to joint possession or enjoyment of the house, preventing strangers from entering family residences.

faqs.question: How do I stop someone from building on undivided ancestral land?
faqs.answer: You must immediately file a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) in the Civil Court along with an application for a Temporary Injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The court will issue an injunction restraining all construction.

faqs.question: What is the Pre-emption (Ogrokroy) right in ancestral land?
faqs.answer: Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, when a co-sharer sells their agricultural land share to a stranger, the other co-heirs have the legal right to apply to court to buy back that share at the registered price plus statutory compensation.

faqs.question: Can a co-heir sell a specific portion (e.g., roadside land) before partition?
faqs.answer: No. Before a formal partition deed or civil court decree, all co-heirs own undivided interests across the entire land. A sale of a specific demarcated plot without consent is legally void regarding that demarcation, and the buyer only gets an undivided fractional share.

faqs.question: How long does a Partition Suit (Batwara Mamla) take in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: A contested Partition Suit generally takes between 1 to 3 years, proceeding through a preliminary decree of shares, appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for physical surveying, and issuance of a final partition decree.

faqs.question: Do married daughters have the same land rights as sons in ancestral property?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Islamic inheritance law, daughters have statutory fixed shares in both their father's and mother's estates. Their inheritance rights are permanent and cannot be denied or bypassed on grounds of receiving wedding gifts or dowry.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) stop an illegal ancestral sale from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, empowering a trusted relative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file civil injunctions and partition suits on their behalf.
